original_value: Privacy-preserving data publishing has received much attention in recent years. Prior studies have developed various algorithms such as generalization, anatomy, and L-diversity slicing to protect individuals’ privacy when transactional data are published for public use. These existing algorithms, however, all have certain limitations. For instance, generalization protects identity privacy well but loses a considerable amount of information. Anatomy prevents attribute disclosure and lowers information loss, but fails to protect membership privacy. The more recent probability L-diversity slicing algorithm overcomes some shortcomings of generalization and anatomy, but cannot shield data from more subtle types of attacks such as skewness attack and similarity attack. To meet the demand of data owners with high privacy-preserving requirement, this study develops a novel method named t-closeness slicing (TCS) to better protect transactional data against various attacks. The time complexity of TCS is log-linear, hence the algorithm scales well with large data. We conduct experiments using three transactional data sets and find that TCS not only effectively protects membership privacy, identity privacy, and attribute privacy, but also preserves better data utility than benchmarking algorithms.The online supplement is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/ijoc.2017.0791 .

result.paraphrase: Privacy-preserving data publishing has attracted considerable attention in recent years. Earlier work has proposed a range of algorithms, including generalization, anatomy, and L-diversity slicing, to safeguard individuals’ privacy when transactional data are released for public use. However, each of these approaches has notable limitations. Generalization offers strong identity privacy protection but sacrifices substantial information. Anatomy reduces information loss and protects against attribute disclosure, yet it does not ensure membership privacy. The newer probability L-diversity slicing method addresses some weaknesses of generalization and anatomy, but it still cannot defend against more subtle attacks such as skewness and similarity attacks. To satisfy data owners who require stronger privacy protection, this study introduces a new technique called t-closeness slicing (TCS) for improved defense of transactional data against a variety of attacks. TCS has log-linear time complexity, so it scales efficiently to large datasets. Experiments on three transactional datasets show that TCS effectively protects membership, identity, and attribute privacy while maintaining better data utility than benchmark algorithms. The online supplement is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/ijoc.2017.0791 .
